I was devastated because the curriculum the program was locked into could not at all address the many years of neglect these students had experienced. No amount of extra office hours in a ten week quarter could make up for their history of academic neglect.

comments.name: Candace

From the first paragraph, I read this article with a knot in my throat from fighting the tears welling up in my eyes. I don’t know if you remember me but my son and your daughter attended P.S. 307 together in kindergarten. Faraji, my husband, you and I, at the end of that year, spoke about the educational decisions we made for our children. You and Faraji shared in great detail your plans to stay and fight from within. My husband and I decided to take our son out and place him in a Black private school. Two years later we bought a place in East New York then subsequently moved our sons to the local charter school system, Achievement First. Even with our best efforts and them attending an “academically” sound charter, it’s abundantly clear that moving to one of the worst school districts in Brooklyn in search of the dream of home ownership, my son still did not get the education her deserved. We’re now in a similar situation investing in extra tutoring services to fill in the gaps that were created early on. My husband and I have always been champions and advocates of education but it did not shield our son from the innumerable inequalities associated with educational zip code racism. 

We try our best, Nikole. And in some ways, we will fall short as parents. However, the grit, confidence, and advocacy you instilled in Nayja coupled with with the way she saw you and your husband fight for her gave her one hell of a baseline for greatness.
Very enlightening and thought provoking essay. But, in choosing to send your daughter to a predominantly Black school don’t you ironically perpetuate the segregation you oppose?

comments.name: David
comments.body:
There is a regulation that can be imposed on AI with relatively little effort but lots of impact.

Today, It is still true that every AI agent -- including those that launch other agents -- has a human "parent" -- the living, breathing human who made a conscious decision to click a button that said "LAUNCH", giving birth to the agent.

That human owner's identity should be recorded in a "Agent Birth Certificate" embedded into the agent (and its children) in a standard, cryptographically tamper-proof way.  Then, any computer system asked to provide access or support for the agent should be able to inspect this information, analyze it, contact the owner, or -- if the information is missing or invalid -- deem the agent hostile, deny resources to it, and stop it dead.

Intermediaries and services would spring up to help anyone identify the parent of an agent and decide whether to trust it.

There is still time to mandate that every AI agent be attached to a human (or corporation) at the other end -- the entity that would be strictly liable for any harm done to others by the agent or its children.

But as Ezra's piece suggests, once RSI arrives and AI is making and launching itself, it will be too late.

AI is increasingly being integrated into all kinds of software. If AI were turned off using a kill switch, all kinds of services would come to a standstill. If you think that's not a problem, we might as well just turn off the power supply and achieve the same result.

The goal needs to be that humans will always be in control of A.I. As the current A.I. race hurtles forward, we're approaching a tipping point where that won't be the case. It would be akin to inviting an alien life form with superior intelligence into our world.

The real race isn't between the U.S. and China, but between humanity and A.I. superintelligence. The answer may lie in several different solutions, including a physical kill switch. We do need Congress to address this issue urgently.

However, this wouldn't be my first home which I got before I got sick. That wasn't in an ideal neighborhood with a billboard picture of Captain Morgan staring into my then newborn son's nursery; I've always wondered if that had long term ramifications.

comments.name: robin Perry
comments.body:
We bought our first home  in 2000 when I was 30 in Long Beach, CA. We moved to an area that looked as if its better days had come and gone. The housing stock was old but the neighborhood was walkable had good schools & was close to my office. When we purchased our home for 325,000, many thought we were crazy. Everyone, esspecially, older people, feared that it was too much for what we were getting. Fast-forward. 26 years The same neighborhood is one of the most desirable areas in our city and in fact in our region.. Our house has appreciated by a factor of 5.

I do fear that our adult children could not afford our home or nearly any home in Long Beach. The median price has climbed to almost least $900,000. That is a material change from what it wants was 25 years ago where two income families could buy a house in the region.

A solution is to live further and further away from the economic core. That has significant drawbacks including the commute, and access to economic and cultural opportunities..

The solution has to be building more homes, closer to the urban core and helping young people qualify with smaller down payments. . It’s easy to posit that  young adults are wasteful spenders with different priorities. But that just lets us off the hook for our failure to build sufficient housing like generations  before. “Slow growth”  has maintained  bucolic neighborhoods like mine while excluding the construction of apartments, townhomes, & condominiums that we need.

comments.body:
Back when I was young and fresh out of the Navy it was plain and simple, I did without.  Period.  No week long vacations, no steak dinners out at the popular spot, very limited drinking at bars or other spots,  NO sporting events like hockey, football,baseball. College or professional, no trips to gamble in Vegas, kept a used car at least 7-10 more years ( i worked in them, oil, filters, brakes, plugs, 

I painted any rental place with the owners permission if needed and worked out a deal to take money off my rent etc 

When I did get my first home, I did all the maintenance, the exterior and interior painting, lawn, minor concrete work.  Did my own maintenance on HVAC, still worked on my car.  

Guess what?  It all paid off. I can now do want I want, when I want and take a vacation wherever I want to go.  

The biggest success? I can review a contractor’s estimate, hire him or tell him to take a hike,  go overcharge some other person who never took the time to learn how to do anything themselves.

Part of the Trumpian atmosphere is the militarization of daily life. Everything becomes a chance to demonstrate "toughness", as if it is always possible to out-work your way to some imagined success and approaching anything with a different mindset is a recipe for being exploited. 

If someone in a war zone or in special ops training has to keep going no matter what their bodies are doing, then don't we all have to no matter what we are doing or risk being seen as less tough? Well, according to some people, yes, but those people are not only ignorant, they are either hypocrites or living a life that nearly guarantees misery on all fronts.

 The correct answer is of course not. Learning what is and isn't an emergency is a valuable life skill - and part of protecting oneself from manipulation by the unfortunate souls who act as if they cannot.

No one at the University has taken responsibility for this preventable tragedy, and there is no criminal investigation. It appears the cover-up is well underway at the university.

comments.name: Amy
comments.body: I’m sure I heard just this past August-September of another football player dropping (dead?) from heat stroke.   Why are coaches, schools, owners, competition organizers against bringing training indoors on days they know the athletes are at risk of overheating?  Or, establishing fines when an athlete continues in a competition when they know they’re about to release bodily fluids, and then do so on the course. We charge D.U.I drivers when they kill an innocent driver or pedestrian. Why are we allowing stone cold sober coaches, schools, owners, and competition organizers off the hook? They are not responsible for everything that happens to an athlete or goes wrong at a competitive event. But they are responsible for acting like the leaders their titles suggest they are.

comments.name: Michael Smith
comments.body:
I live in Australia. The sports culture here is extreme. It begins at a very young age and often involves a lot of bullying and cheating. Parents are heavily invested in their children’s future professional sporting success, and will engage in all sorts of unedifying behaviour on the sidelines. Living through one’s children is a vicarious form of narcissism, and it’s widespread.

I’m of South Asian extraction, and our equivalent of sporting hyper competition is academics. It is equally ruthless and no less damaging. I’ve seen individuals and families destroyed by the toxicity of constantly wanting to be seen as superior to everyone else.

In both endeavours, people are constantly learning how to play the system. They aren’t necessarily the best at what they do. I had to make a conscious effort not to repeat my parent’s mistakes when raising my son. This wasn’t easy as there’s no manual for that.

But I’m happy to report that it’s an approach that pays dividends - for parents and young people.

comments.body: Jessica, thank you for mentioning the NFL and the deadly impact of repeated concussions suffered by NFL players. All the while, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has earned over $700 million in that role, and just signed a new contract through 2030.

comments.name: Guy Carden
comments.body:
“The repellent images ... so outlandish and so viscerally off-putting ... a noxious mark on her road to victory ... Wietrzyk and Hyrox  ... made unconditional apologies ... Wietrzyk retroactively withdrew from the race...”

I agree with Ms. Grose that American sports culture is unhinged in important ways,  and that football is a glaring example. Brain damage is a real risk at all levels of tackle football, and it is shocking that the sport continues essentially unchanged.

The Hyrox incident is not comparable.

It is said that cleanliness is next to Godliness,  but it is possible to be too delicate.  Has Ms. Grose ever changed a diaper?  Ever had diarrhea?  Ever had a partner who had diarrhea?  Ever cleaned up after a neighbor’s dog?

Were there health or safety risks?  Did Ms. Wietrzyk interfere with her competitors?  Yes, but at a very minor level:  Some competitors reported that they had slipped on the damp spot. Apparently no one reported seeing contamination on shared equipment. Hyrox claims they have an “emergency response protocol for biological contamination incidents”, so things presumably got cleaned up.

Nothing here compares to the chronic traumatic encephalopathy or heat stroke cases Ms.Gross talks about.

Personally, I think that Ms. Wietrzyk was right to continue the race, and I congratulate her on her win.

comments.name: Nana (sage)
comments.body: Sports has lost the plot. It teaches children and teens discipline, cooperation, competition, working in teams to accomplish a goal that sets the tone for cooperation with others in life and a healthy body that through evolution is made to move and be celebrated. As an athlete I also learned how to lose with grace and celebrate my wins with humility knowing that fortune and luck in any given day was a gift and not permanent. These are the things most of us learned in sports ( I was a swimmer who competed throughout my life and at UCLA) and carried that love of sport through my adult life in other sports. Let’s recalibrate how we look at this. The money is ruining everything. Not just sports.

If he and his colleagues are successful in convincing enough of the superannuated to shun vaccinations for things such as the flu, pneumonia, cancers and covid, natural selection will take care of the rest.  Many will say this is cold, calculating and callous, but the fact is we simply do not have enough money, no one wants to take care of a bunch of old sick people for just peanuts, the national debt is ballooning and countless Americans, especially job creators, are demanding tax relief.  So, let’s move forward and tackle these more pressing problems.  No doubt socialists would do things differently but socialism is something we most definitely can’t afford.

comments.name: anon

I have lived in 6 countries and while every system has problems, what goes on in the USA, in my opinion, the worst of the lot. Heath care should be like having water, electricity... it should be considered a right and not a privilege. 

I sometimes cynically think that the actual plan to help balance the federal budget is to kill the elderly sooner. Then they'd save on medicare A&B, SNAP, HUD, Medicaid, and social security. Certainly not having the help needed for people as they age is going to cause some to die younger than they would otherwise.

What is discussed in this article is only going to get worse. The youngest of the baby boom generation only turns 62 in 2026. And while many of the older boomers will have died by the time they reach 80, being followed by the baby bust generation still leaves numerous problems since having fewer of the generation below the boomers pay into annuities, etc. means that entire system is less solvent. Already some companies have commented about that. 

And singles or people with no kids are likely to have the most problems since they will need to pay for more of their care that in other circumstances families help with/pay for.

comments.name: Bill Horan

"There are also cots and showers for technicians who might hunker down during extreme weather to keep the servers running."

From one nerd to another, keep a "Go Bag" in your car with a few home comforts like a freshly laundered sleeping bag and inflatable foam camping mattress, change of clothes, fresh shoes or slippers, snacks and MREs, a couple of books, chargers and cables, etc.

I once spent a week at a snowed in mountaintop transmitter site, and my Go Bag made it much more comfortable.  The only comforts my coworker had was sharing food I'd brought, and dreams of all the overtime.

It sounds small, but that’s the difference between six minutes of outage a year and 30 seconds. 

Better check your figures.

There are roughly 31.5 million seconds in a solar year. 1/100000th of that is 315 seconds, or 5min 15sec. 1 millionth of a year is 31.5 seconds. Had you written "It sounds small, but that’s the difference between five minutes of outage a year and 30 seconds", I might have ignored the small inaccuracy. But saying, in effect, that "10 = 12" is a bridge too far for me,

comments.name: Tom Gooch

This is a fascinating piece. It reminds me that a prejudice of the modern world is that only sense experience can tell us what is real. But that's an unwarranted assumption, as the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead showed in great detail. 

If the only thing "real" in the universe is what we can pick up with our five senses, we are living in a diminished world. If, on the other hand, we take the "real" to be what we actually experience, then that experience is far more than what five senses can report on. The world we experience is one in which it's completely reasonable to have the kind of nonsensory experiences this author describes. 

My hunch is that the universe as it really is is far more surprising and fabulous than we are schooled to believe.

(Of course, if I'm wrong, and I find myself standing at a gate in front of a guy with long white hair, a beard, wearing a robe and opening a book with my name on it, I'm really going to be surprised. Death is nothing at all.
I have only slipped away to the next room.
I am I and you are you.
Whatever we were to each other,
That, we still are.

Call me by my old familiar name.
Speak to me in the easy way
which you always used.
Put no difference into your tone.
Wear no forced air of solemnity or sorrow.

Laugh as we always laughed
at the little jokes we enjoyed together.
Play, smile, think of me. Pray for me.
Let my name be ever the household word
that it always was.
Let it be spoken without effect.
Without the trace of a shadow on it.

Life means all that it ever meant.
It is the same that it ever was.
There is absolute unbroken continuity.
Why should I be out of mind
because I am out of sight?

I am but waiting for you.
For an interval.
Somewhere. Very near.
Just around the corner.

All is well.

--Henry Scott Holland

It is not at all surprising that mourners long to believe the loss of their loved ones is not permanent, that the dead live on in an afterlife, and that the living will be reunited with those they have lost in the fullness of time.  Nor is it surprising to learn that intimations of the persistence of those who have died bring relief to mourners.  How comforting it must be to believe that your dead child still exists, albeit on a different plane, and that the connection between you can never be severed.  It isn't at all difficult to imagine the subconscious mind finding the "evidence" needed to sustain this belief.  

Does this mean that persons who believe in communications from beyond the grave are delusional?  Well, yes, if they insist that they possess factual proof of the afterlife.  You probably don't want to make life-changing decisions based on the alleged testimony of the recently deceased.  But as a mechanism for coping with grief, finding echoes of loved ones in familiar objects and surprising coincidences seems to have been therapeutic for the author of this essay and the others whose experiences she describes.

My father died suddenly when I was 19. I was in college and the previous weekend I had been visiting at home. When the time came for me to go back to college my father was not home. I could have waited a bit longer until he came back but I didn't. I thought I was going to see him the next weekend, or the other. That weekend never came. On Thursday he was gone. 
For a long time I felt guilty because I had not stayed until he came back so I could say goodbye. It was a sorrow I carried with me and I knew I could not go back in time and change things.
I cannot remember specifically when it happened, but it was years latter. One night I had a dream in which I was with my beloved father and it was so real that I thought I know this is a dream but I don't want it to end. I was in a state between sleep and alert. I was so happy to see him again and I knew I was having my opportunity to say goodbye.
After that day I no longer felt guilty. I cherish that dream in my mind as my last moment with my father. I don't know what type of experience it was but for me it was very real and of this world.
I am a doctor, older than my father was when he died and when they ask for my religion I check None. So I don't believe in magic. But I believe in connections that survive us.

The necklace story: I was wondering if the woman who gave the necklace to the MD story teller may have been from another culture?

My husband professor traveled the world for about 15 years, because our area of research (the development of "youth," roughly ages 18-30) is often of greater interest to other countries than in our country). 

In a couple of his early trips abroad--often to developing nations--he was unfamiliar with a country's customs. One time he was in the Middle East and complimented a man on his tie at a conference. The man took off the tie and gave to husband. 

Husband felt embarrassed, tried to give it back, but the man seemed genuinely upset and refused to take it back. A few years later, it happened again when husband complimented a man on a pouch he was carrying, so the man gives him the pouch. 

Then husband saw the cultural pattern--that giving someone a compliment may obligate them to show their generosity (seemingly happy to do so). Lovely custom.

Husband was traveling in a hot, humid country and someone from an African country at a conference complimented him on his LL Bean madras shirt. So husband took it off and gave it to him; and the fellow seemed quite delighted and remained friendly throughout the conference. 

Somewhere in between, husband learned to take an assortment of little gifts to give others on his trips.

Husband is 91. We have moved 3 times since we retired, and some of those gifts (esp. the lovely necktie) move with us.

I sometimes get polite comments on my clothing, and I much appreciate the compliments. But I suspect this is because I sew many of my own clothes (being the size of a 12 year old for decades now has required this), and so they fit quite well. 

That said, the item of clothing I get the greatest number of compliments about is a coat I received from a dear relative who sewed it more than 50 years ago now.

It is a beautiful corduroy, multi-colored patchwork coat, knee length, and fully lined with satin. I've even had a few women ask if they might buy it from me! If it weren't from a relative, I might consider being a bit more generous, but this is one item of clothing I'll never part with.

This relative, a step-great-aunt, to be precise, was one of those older relatives all kids should have. This was Aunt Blanche. Understanding, able to soothe all the hurts that come with childhood, and yet requiring the highest of standards in any undertaking. 

Oh, and she did have a quirky sense of humor. One of her grandchildren and I were the only two kids in any branch of her family who were quite studious. We were also the "odd kids out" because I was "only" step-family, and he was adopted. Because of this, she often said of me and of this grandchild that the smartest two people in their family weren't related to them.....

Wishing everyone here on the MD stoop a wonderful week,
OC

China’s greatest advantage today may not simply be Xi’s growing power, but America’s willingness to weaken its own position.
Beijing already has formidable structural advantages: dominance in rare-earth processing, enormous manufacturing capacity, increasingly sophisticated technology and the ability to impose real economic costs on the United States. Those advantages become even more valuable when Washington alienates allies, consumes military resources elsewhere and launches trade wars before reducing its dependence on Chinese supply chains.

Trump did not create China’s rise, and America retains enormous strengths in technology, finance, military power and alliances. But those strengths are less useful when Washington undermines the very alliances and international confidence that amplify them.

comments.name: Alex A
comments.body:
Companies that provide for betting such as Polymarket are indeed vulnerable to fraud. Even with regulation and good business practices this may be hard to prevent.

 

The greater risk is that they are vulnerable to insider trading and market manipulation. I don't see how these risks can be effectively managed. There is a substantial risk that those with implicit or explicit insider information may make wagers benefiting themselves at the expense of honest participants. The greater and more consequential risk is probably market manipulation, whereas those with the ability to influence outcomes may attempt to do so. This could happen in financial markets; perhaps the greater danger is that it could occur in situations that affect public policy, or even military situations. I don't stay awake at night worrying that adults may lose money to insider trading; as the saying goes, fools and their money are soon parted. I do worry about market manipulation that may have much wider effect.

 

I do not believe prediction markets such as Polyymarket serve a useful societal function.  I believe they should be outlawed in this country, or at the very least heavily regulated and appropriately taxed.

 

I also believe it is inappropriate for Dow Jones to have a contractual relationship with Polymarket. Though the reporting in this article seems thorough and impartial, I believe the relationship undermines the reputation and impartiality of the Journal.

The contract is lopsided against Guyana - and the OCs are making a killing on the oil extraction business, thanks to a lopsided contract that came into being through fraud. Minister Trotman who signed it in 2016 said he had been "instructed" to sign by an unnamed person. It was an underhand deal between an unnamed person and an official of Exxon. 

Guyana needs a fair oil contract. It should be renegotiated to provide at least 6.25% royalty (same as Suriname's oil contract, all things being equal) + 50% share of Windfall profits whenever there is a war.
 
On royalty alone Guyana loses $37.4 billion (compared to Suriname's royalty rate): Simple Math: 11-billion-barrel reserve times 4.25% times av price per barrel $80 = $37.4 billion.

Almost the exact same story here--I was on the SAVE plan and in June 2024 was put on administrative forbearance with 116/120 payments towards PSLF. I almost immediately tried to switch to a new payment plan (Income-Driven Repayment), which sat unanswered for several months (on my student loan page, it still says "recalculating" for that request).

Eventually I called Mohela for assistance. When calling to request to be put on a new plan, the representative said that they were "working in batches" and I wasn't part of the batch. I then requested a PSLF buyback from the Department of Education, which I have never heard back about.

Ultimately I had to file a second request for being placed on IDR, which for some reason this time worked. I finished paying off the last few payments and received forgiveness.

The story isn't quite over--when you get PSLF, while you wait for final approval you can elect to enter forbearance until it is approved, or you can continue paying your monthly payments and receive a refund from the US Treasury after PSLF is approved. Given my issues with forbearance in the past, I elected to continue paying. I have two or three months of continued payments that, several months later, I have not been reimbursed for. Mohela notes that it has no responsibility for this, and the federal government has no apparent recourse or contact point for the return of these thousands of dollars. So I suppose I just wait.

There must be a more effective solution than this.

Exceptional tribute. Thank you. I agree that she lives forever in us. I read her astonishing “Total Eclipse” as a prelude to seeing the 2017 Total Eclipse in Oregon, my first. Being in Totality for nearly a minute changed my life as did the essay. 

The line: “We were born and bored at a stroke” seems a perfect synopsis of life as a Dillard reader.

comments.name: Erika
comments.body:
Thank you for this. Holy the Firm and The Maytrees are two of my favorite books of all time. Her sentences were poems, their rhythms like dance. There’s a passage in the Maytrees where the stoic, bookish main character reflects on the great love she has for her son as he is about to head off into his own adult life. She describes setting a table for each of the various iterations of him over the years. She knows each of him so well — his favorite foods, his moods, his habits. They are, each of him, fully whole separate people. It’s a passage that comes to mind every time I or someone close to me have lost someone we loved. Somehow the pain of their absence is eased just a little by that crowded table full of them; all the years and experiences of them now gathered together for us. 

And now each place at the table seats another of her beautiful books and essays, alive and immediate, timeless and ready to greet us like a Puget Sound day. Newborn and salted, the day’s god “…flings his arms, spreading colors; he arches, cupping sky in his belly; he vaults, vaulting and spread, holding all and spread on me like skin.”

Metaphorical magic is what I felt, decades ago, as a little girl holding my first library card next to a stack of books I was checking out, all genres of books that opened the world to me, and it is what I felt when I read to my own children, and they first read out loud, then also grew-up to become voracious readers.

I remember back in 2014, Lev Shlosberg began to suffer persecution for being the first to sound the alarm that the regiment in Pskov were not in their barracks and were...somewhere...which turned out to be Crimea. They were busy forcibly annexing it to Russia. Lev was severely beaten and hospitalized after reporting on the first soldiers' funerals from the war on Ukraine.
